analysis.investment_thesis: Aavas Financiers built an admirable seven-year track record in rural affordable housing (22% revenue CAGR, 30% PAT CAGR) but revenue has now stalled — INR 2,018 Cr in 2024 versus INR 1,988 Cr in 2025 — and ROE of 13.9% falls short of my 15% hurdle. The forward P/E of 13.6x is attractive only if growth genuinely re-accelerates.
key_strengths: Net profit CAGR of 29.7% over seven years (INR 93 Cr → INR 574 Cr) demonstrating sustained execution in an underpenetrated market
Strong institutional confidence with 24.7% FII and 14.3% DII ownership, and P/B of 2.28x implies market trusts the book quality
Minimal capex requirements (INR 30 Cr/year) — the business is capital-light at the fixed-asset level even if leveraged at the loan-book level
key_risks: Revenue growth has stalled: FY25 revenue of INR 1,988 Cr is below FY24's INR 2,018 Cr — a warning signal for a high-growth lender
ROE of 13.9% is below my minimum 15% threshold and declining, with D/E of 3.08x among the highest in the peer group
Heavy reliance on external borrowings (INR 13,918 Cr debt vs INR 4,361 Cr equity) means refinancing risk and rate-cycle sensitivity are real
red_flags: OCF negative every single year for five years (0/5 positive); INR -1,660 Cr in FY25 — the business consumes cash relentlessly
Finance cost data for 2025 shows only INR 5 Cr versus INR 828 Cr in 2024 — this appears to be a data anomaly and obscures true cost of funds analysis
Promoter holding of 48.95% is relatively modest for a financial firm; FII at 24.7% means any sentiment shift triggers outsized selling
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aavas has done many things right: disciplined underwriting in self-employed rural borrowers, consistent profit growth, and lean fixed-cost infrastructure. But a growth HFC that stops growing revenue is a different animal — the leveraged business model requires continuous loan-book expansion to cover fixed funding costs and justify the P/B premium. The stall in FY25 demands explanation before I commit capital.

At 21.8x trailing P/E and 13.6x forward P/E, the stock prices in a return to 20%+ PAT growth. Given ROE of 13.9% and flat revenue, I cannot yet see the engine that drives that recovery. I would revisit at INR 1,000–1,100 (roughly 10–11x forward earnings) where the margin of safety compensates for the execution uncertainty. Today, I watch and wait.
